extracted.intended_audience: general readers and skeptics interested in the historical/authorship credibility of Biblical books; readers of Thomas Paine and deistic criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methods for judging whether books of the Bible were written by their ascribed authors and whether the texts are historically authoritative, using internal textual evidence (anachronisms, tense, narration, contradictions, omissions, moral content, and verbatim borrowing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship contradicted by references to later events
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book refers to events, places, or conditions that occurred after the purported author's death, it could not have been written by that author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Exodus xvi.35 (manna eaten until they came to the borders of Canaan) extends into Joshua's time though Moses died before entering Canaan; Joshua xxiv.31 speaks of what people did after Joshua's death. Such post-dated references are positive evidence the book was composed later than the ascribed author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim borrowing / textual duplication as evidence of later composition
rubrics_metrics.description: When passages are word-for-word identical across books, the later book (or the compiler) likely copied from the other, implying later composition for the copier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Genesis xxxvi. and 1 Chronicles i. contain verbatim overlapping verses; Paine infers Genesis drew from Chronicles, making Genesis later than the events it purports to record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of preterite tense incompatible with prophetic authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions rendered in the past tense ('preter tense') that purport to be prophetic statements indicate they were written after the events, undermining claims of genuine prophecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine notes passages where the language is in the preterite and argues it would be 'downright idiotism' to claim a man prophesied in the preterite — e.g., references to pursuing them unto Dan and later kings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronistic geographic/artifactual references (e.g., Rabbah, 'bedstead of Og')
rubrics_metrics.description: References to locations, relics, or possessions that only became known or relevant centuries later indicate the writer lived after those later events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Deuteronomy iii.11 refers to Og's bed at Rabbah; Rabbah was not taken until Joab's campaign ~400 years later, so the reference implies later knowledge and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person narration inconsistent with claimed first-person authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: When a work ascribed to a named individual is written in third person (an historian recounting 'he did X') rather than first person, that inconsistency undermines the claim that the named person authored it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine observes Joshua is narrated in the third person (the historian of Joshua speaks) making it absurd to suppose Joshua himself wrote the book attributed to him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory glosses for archaic terms indicate later author
rubrics_metrics.description: When a text explains terms that were current in the purported original period, it suggests the writer lived later and felt the need to explain archaic usage to contemporary readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1 Samuel explains that 'he that is now called a prophet, was before-time called a seer,' which Paine reads as the later writer explaining an older term to his contemporaries—evidence of later composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological contradictions across books
rubrics_metrics.description: Differing or conflicting chronological statements in parallel histories (different reign years, sequences) indicate unreliable historical authorship and later compilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Conflicting statements about the reign-starts of Joram/Jehoram in 2 Kings (one place says second year, another says fifth year) show internal chronological contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission or silence about prominent contemporaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure of a historical book to mention prophets or prominent figures who should, by chronology, appear in its narrative suggests selective composition, later editing, or unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine notes many prophets (Hosea, Amos, Micah, etc.) are unmentioned in Kings/Chronicles despite living before those histories were written; such silence is suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference of content between parallel histories implies multiple compilers
rubrics_metrics.description: When two histories of the same events differ markedly—one including sensational miracles and the other silent—this suggests they were written by different anonymous authors and compiled later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kings contains tales of Elijah's ascent in a chariot of fire and Elisha's miracles; Chronicles mentions Elijah but omits these sensational stories, indicating differing authorship and selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of fables, miracles, and mythic elements undermines historical credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that resemble fables or mythology (giants, miraculous halting of sun/moon, extreme lifespans) lower the text's claim to sober history or divine revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine compares the story of the sun standing still and the long lifespans in Genesis to Arabian Tales or Homeric mythology, arguing such fantastical elements make the accounts 'only fit to amuse children' and not historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of immoral or cruel orders to the deity undermines divine authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: If a text ascribes extreme cruelty, massacres, or morally abhorrent orders to God or his agents, this casts doubt on claims that the text is divinely authored or morally authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine cites Moses' alleged order to 'kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman that hath known a man,' and other massacres and atrocities (children's heads exposed, ripping up pregnant women) as morally repugnant and incompatible with a benevolent deity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrases like 'unto this day' date the writing to well after the events
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that things 'remain unto this day' indicate the narrator wrote at a time when those relics or conditions still existed, thereby dating the composition to that later time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include repeated uses in Joshua (e.g., 'which remaineth unto this day')—Paine uses these phrases to argue the books were written long after the events they describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal self-contradiction in time/place phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages that imply both contemporaneity and long historical perspective (e.g., saying 'after the death of X' then summarizing 306 years) point to compilation from later sources rather than eyewitness accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine notes Judges begins 'Now after the death of Joshua' but the second chapter is an epitome spanning centuries, indicating the author wrote with later historical perspective, not as immediate witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity equals lack of authoritative provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book lacks an ascribed, credible author (is anonymous), it lacks the nominal voucher that would support claims of divine inspiration or historical authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine repeatedly emphasizes that many books (e.g., Judges, Genesis as compiled) are anonymous and therefore 'without authority'—he treats anonymity as a disqualifying feature for claiming divine origin.
